title: Xiangyan Strikes the Bamboo
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Chan Master Xiangyan Zhixian was a native of Qingzhou. Weary of the secular world, he took leave of his parents and traveled about in search of the Way. While at Baizhang’s, though naturally intelligent and acute, he could not gain Chan through meditation. When (jì, “when, until”) Baizhang passed away, he went to study under Guishan (an eminent monk of the Tang dynasty, the first patriarch of the Guiyang school). inline.s: Chan Master Xiangyan Zhixian was a native of Qingzhou. Weary of the secular world, he took leave of his parents and traveled about observing the regions in search of the Way. While at Baizhang’s, though naturally intelligent and acute, he could not gain Chan through meditation. When
jì
, “when, until”)
Baizhang passed away
(when Chan Master Baizhang died)
, he went to study under Guishan
(an eminent monk of the Tang dynasty and the first patriarch of the Guiyang school)

. Guishan asked: “I hear that at my late master Baizhang’s you answered ten for one and a hundred for ten — that is your cleverness and sharp wits. Intellectual understanding and conceptual thinking are
(namely)

the very root of birth and death. Before your father and mother were born, try saying a single phrase!” At this one question the Master was utterly at a loss. He returned to his quarters and, taking the texts he had ordinarily

read, searched through them from beginning to end for a single phrase to answer with, yet could find none. He sighed to himself: “A painted cake cannot satisfy hunger.” Again and again he begged Guishan to explain it outright. Guishan said: “If I were to explain it for you,
(if I were to lay it bare for you)
you would curse me later. What I say is mine; it has nothing to do with you.”

The Master thereupon burned all the texts he had been reading, saying: “In this life I will study no more Buddhist doctrine. Let me simply be a long-wandering gruel-and-rice monk, and spare my mind and spirit.” Weeping, he took leave of Guishan. Passing straight through Nanyang, he came upon the traces of National Teacher Zhong
(National Teacher Huizhong)
, and there he rested and stayed. One day, as he was cutting
shān
, “to cut grass”)
away the grass and brush, he happened to toss a piece of tile, which struck the bamboo with a sound — and suddenly he was awakened. He hastened
jù
, “hastily”)

back, bathed, burned incense, bowed toward Guishan from afar, and praised him, saying: “Your great compassion, O Venerable, exceeds even a parent’s kindness. Had you explained it to me then, how could there be today’s affair?”
Then he composed a verse: “One strike and all that is known is forgotten — no further cultivation is needed. Every motion reveals the ancient path
(every motion proclaims the way of the ancient sages — seeing the nature and becoming Buddha)
, never falling into the trap of silent stillness
(not idly guarding barren stillness)
. Nowhere are there any traces
(the wondrous essence of the true mind)
; a bearing beyond sound and form
(the dignity of the true mind’s wondrous essence transcends sound and form
). Those who have attained the Way everywhere all say
(all say)
it is of the very highest capacity.”
When Guishan heard of this, he said to Yangshan: “This lad has penetrated
(has had the great awakening)
.” Yangshan said: “That is just the workings of mind and conceptual consciousness, composed into verse. Wait until I
have personally tested him.” Later Yangshan met the Master and said: “The Venerable
(Guishan)
praises you, junior brother, for having brought to light the great matter
(illuminating the mind and seeing the nature)

. Try speaking and let me see.” The Master recited his previous verse. Yangshan said: “That is composed from habit-energy and memory; if you have truly awakened, speak of something else.” The Master then composed another verse: “Last year’s poverty was not yet poverty; this year’s poverty is poverty indeed. Last year’s poverty still had ground enough to plant an awl
(to stand an awl)
(the state where the myriad thoughts return to one)
; this year’s poverty, not even the awl remains
(not even ground to stand an awl — the state where the single thought returns to nothing)
.” Yangshan said: “The Tathagata Chan, I grant that you, junior brother, have understood. But the Patriarchal Chan, you have not yet seen even in a dream.” The Master then made another verse:
I have a mechanism
(I have a contrivance)
; with a blink of the eye I see it
(a blink and one can see it)
. If a person does not understand
(if one cannot grasp it)
, turn and call the novice
(turn the head and call the novice: drag out this corpse)
Yangshan
(Yangshan)
then reported to Guishan: “I rejoice that our brother Xian
(Zhixian)
has understood the Patriarchal Chan.”
(The Wudeng Yantong)

[Tathagata Chan] This refers to the Chan methods prevalent in China before Bodhidharma came from the West — for example, the Chan of counting the breath (ānāpāna), the Chan of the five gates, and so on. Their characteristic is: cultivating contemplation in accordance with the teachings, gathering the mind into samādhi, and advocating liberation through meditation. [Patriarchal Chan] This refers to the Chan transmitted by Patriarch Bodhidharma: not setting up words and letters, a special transmission outside the teachings, directly pointing to the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming Buddha. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “It speaks only of seeing the nature, not of meditation and liberation.” [Special transmission outside the teachings] The Chan school does not establish words and letters nor set up phrases, but directly transmits the mind-seal of the Buddhas and patriarchs; this is called “a special transmission outside the teachings,” meaning a special transmission apart from the verbal teachings of the Tathagata. The Sutra of the Great Brahma King Asking the Buddha to Resolve His Doubts relates that Brahma came to Vulture Peak and offered the Buddha a golden utpala flower, begging him to teach the Dharma. Śākyamuni held up the flower before the assembly but did not speak; for a time the millions of gods and humans could not grasp his meaning, and only the Venerable Kāśyapa broke into a subtle smile. The World-Honored One said: “I have the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the true form that is formless, the subtle and wondrous Dharma gate that does not set up words and letters, a special transmission outside the teachings. This I entrust to Mahākāśyapa.” This is the origin of the Chan school. Thus Patriarchal Chan also originates from the Tathagata, only it is a special transmission outside the teachings. [Treasury of the true Dharma eye] The Buddha’s mind-eye penetratingly sees the true Dharma — this is called the “true Dharma eye”; it is profound, vast, and contains myriad virtues, hence it is called a “treasury.”

[I have a mechanism] The body and mind of the five aggregates are often likened to a wooden puppet driven by a mechanism (a wooden man driven by a contrivance). The “mechanism” in the line “I have a mechanism” is a simile for the contrivance (the self-nature) that drives the puppet (the body and mind of the five aggregates). The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: “There is no maker at all — is this affair an illusion? Is it a wooden puppet, or is it a matter in a dream?” The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “Though one sees the faculties move, it is by one mechanism they are drawn; when the mechanism stops and returns to stillness, all illusions become without self-nature.” [With a blink of the eye I see it] This is the state spoken of by the Fifth Patriarch Hongren in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch: “One who has seen the nature must see it the instant it is spoken (as soon as it is said, one sees).” Therefore Yangshan confirmed that Xiangyan had understood the Patriarchal Chan. [The instant it is spoken] At a single word; immediately. [Turn and call the novice] “Turn” means to twist or turn away. “Turn and call the novice” — turn the head and call the novice: drag out this corpse
(drag out this corpse)! — Here Xiangyan skillfully used an allusion to Yangshan himself.

The Record of Chan Master Yangshan Huiji of Yuanzhou records: When the Master (Yangshan) was a novice, a monk asked Shishuang: “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?” Shishuang said: “It is like a man in a thousand-foot well who can get out without using an inch of rope — that man can answer your question about the meaning of the West.” The monk said: “Recently Venerable Chang of Hunan has appeared in the world, and he too talks east and west for people.” Shishuang called the novice (Yangshan): “Drag out this corpse!” Later the Master asked Danyuan: “How does one get the man in the well out?” Danyuan said: “Bah, you fool! Who is in the well?” The Master then went to ask Guishan. Guishan called: “Huiji (Yangshan’s name)!” The Master answered. Guishan said: “He’s out!” Later, after the Master had taken up residence, he would often cite this exchange, telling the assembly: “I gained my name at Danyuan’s, and my ground at Guishan’s.”
